header:
Why mortgage rates hit 7.28%
and the bond yield behind it

lines.text: On Oct 1, 2026, mortgage rates hit 7.28%.
lines.say: On October first, mortgage rates hit seven point two eight percent.

lines.text: On Feb 26, 2026, they were 5.98%. On a $400,000 loan, that gap is about $344 a month.
lines.say: Back on February twenty-sixth, they were five point nine eight percent. On a four hundred thousand dollar loan, that gap is about three hundred forty-four dollars a month.

lines.text: The reason sits underneath: the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34% on Oct 1, its highest since 2002 (Reuters).
lines.say: The reason sits underneath your mortgage. On October first, the ten-year Treasury yield touched five point three four percent, its highest level since twenty oh two, Reuters reported.

lines.text: And it's not only America. Bond yields in Japan, Britain and Germany hit multi-year highs in September 2026.
lines.say: And it isn't only America. Bond yields in Japan, Britain and Germany also hit multi-year highs in September.

lines.text: That yield is basically the price of borrowing money, and it leaks into almost every loan you can take.
lines.say: That yield is basically the price of borrowing money, and it leaks into almost every loan a person can take.

lines.text: So here's the plan: what a yield is, why it jumped, who wins, who loses, and what to watch next.
lines.say: So here's the plan. What a yield actually is, why it jumped, who wins, who loses, and which dates to watch next.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What happened.
lines.say: Let's start with what happened.

lines.text: On Thursday, Oct 1, 2026, the 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2002, Reuters reported.
lines.say: On Thursday, October first, Reuters reported that the ten-year Treasury yield had climbed to its highest level since twenty oh two.

lines.text: It touched about 5.34% that morning, then buyers stepped in and it eased to about 5.24% later in the day.
lines.say: It touched about five point three four percent that morning. Then buyers stepped in, and it eased to about five point two four percent later in the day.

lines.text: The 30-year Treasury went even higher: about 5.68% on Oct 1, per Tradeweb data cited by The Wall Street Journal.
lines.say: The thirty-year Treasury went even higher, to about five point six eight percent on October first, according to Tradeweb data cited by The Wall Street Journal.

lines.text: This didn't happen overnight. On Sept 15, 2026, the 10-year rose as high as 5.04%, then its highest since 2007, CNBC reported.
lines.say: This didn't happen overnight. On September fifteenth, the ten-year rose as high as five point oh four percent, which was then its highest since twenty oh seven, CNBC reported.

lines.text: On Oct 1, Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 7.28%, up from 7.03% a week earlier.
lines.say: Back to October first. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average thirty-year fixed mortgage at seven point two eight percent, up from seven point oh three percent a week earlier.

lines.text: That's the highest average since November 2023. A year earlier, it was 6.34%.
lines.say: That's the highest average since November twenty twenty-three. A year earlier, it was six point three four percent.

lines.text: Shorter loans moved too: the 15-year fixed averaged 6.60%, up from 6.42% a week earlier.
lines.say: Shorter loans moved too. The fifteen-year fixed averaged six point six oh percent, up from six point four two percent a week earlier.

lines.text: Here's 2026 so far, using Freddie Mac's last survey of each month, plus Oct 1.
lines.say: Here's twenty twenty-six so far, using Freddie Mac's last survey of each month, plus October first.

lines.text: On Feb 26, the rate dipped to 5.98%, under 6% for the first time in about three and a half years.
lines.say: On February twenty-sixth, the rate dipped to five point nine eight percent. That was under six percent for the first time in about three and a half years.

lines.text: Then it climbed, crossed 7% on Sept 24, and jumped again to 7.28% one week later.
lines.say: Then it climbed, crossed seven percent on September twenty-fourth, and jumped again to seven point two eight percent one week later.

lines.text: Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury yield plus a cushion for lenders. On Oct 1, the gap was about 2 points.
lines.say: Mortgage rates tend to follow the ten-year Treasury yield, plus a cushion for lenders. On October first, that gap was about two points.

lines.text: Two weeks earlier, on Sept 16, 2026, the Fed raised its key rate to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike since July 2023.
lines.say: All this came two weeks after the Federal Reserve raised its key rate to a range of three point seven five to four percent on September sixteenth. That was its first hike since July twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: The Fed's statement was short: "Inflation remains elevated."
lines.say: The Fed's statement was short and blunt. Quote, inflation remains elevated.

lines.text: And people feel it. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell to 81.9 in September, its lowest since 2014.
lines.say: And people feel it. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell to eighty-one point nine in September, its lowest reading since twenty fourteen.

lines.text: In that same survey, people expected prices to rise 6.1% over the next 12 months, on average.
lines.say: In that same survey, people expected prices to rise six point one percent over the next twelve months, on average.

lines.text: Chapter 2: How bonds work.
lines.say: So what is this yield everyone's watching?

lines.text: A Treasury is an IOU from the US government. You lend it money, and it pays you interest.
lines.say: A Treasury is basically an IOU from the US government. You lend it money, and it pays you interest until it pays you back.

lines.text: The yield is the yearly return a buyer gets for lending at today's price.
lines.say: The yield is the yearly return a buyer gets for lending at today's price.

lines.text: Here's the twist: when new bonds pay more, old bonds that pay less lose value.
lines.say: Here's the twist. When new bonds start paying more, the old bonds that pay less lose value.

lines.text: Think of it like a seesaw. When lenders demand more to lend, the price of the IOU has to drop.
lines.say: Think of it like a seesaw. When lenders demand more to lend, the price of the IOU has to drop.

lines.text: Example: you own a $1,000, 10-year bond paying 4%. New ones now pay about 5.3%.
lines.say: Here's a made-up example. Say you own a one thousand dollar, ten-year bond paying four percent. New ones now pay about five point three percent.

lines.text: Any buyer would pick the new one, so yours only sells at a discount.
lines.say: Any buyer would pick the new one, so yours only sells at a discount.

lines.text: In this example, its price falls to about $900, so the buyer's return matches about 5.3%.
lines.say: In this example, its price falls to about nine hundred dollars, so the buyer's return works out to about five point three percent.

lines.text: That's why a bond selloff and rising yields are the same story, told from two sides.
lines.say: That's why a bond selloff and rising yields are really the same story, told from two sides.

lines.text: The 10-year matters most because lenders use it as a base for long loans like mortgages.
lines.say: The ten-year matters most because lenders use it as a base for long loans, especially mortgages.

lines.text: It also shapes what companies pay to borrow, and what the government pays on its own debt.
lines.say: It also shapes what companies pay to borrow, and what the government pays on its own debt.

lines.text: And that bill is already huge: the CBO says net interest hit $1,052 billion in the first 11 months of fiscal 2026.
lines.say: And that bill is already huge. The Congressional Budget Office says net interest hit one trillion, fifty-two billion dollars in the first eleven months of fiscal twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: That's up $111 billion, or 12%, from the same stretch a year earlier.
lines.say: That's up one hundred eleven billion dollars, or twelve percent, from the same stretch a year earlier.

lines.text: Higher yields mean every new dollar the US borrows costs more too.
lines.say: Higher yields mean every new dollar the government borrows costs more too.

lines.text: Chapter 3: How we got here.
lines.say: So how did we get here?

lines.text: In late February 2026, when the Iran war began, the 10-year yield was under 4%, CNBC reported.
lines.say: In late February, when the Iran war began, the ten-year yield was under four percent, CNBC reported.

lines.text: On Sept 1, Japan's 10-year yield hit 3% for the first time since 1996.
lines.say: On September first, Japan's ten-year yield hit three percent for the first time since nineteen ninety-six.

lines.text: On Sept 16, the Fed raised rates. And on Oct 1, the US 10-year touched 5.34%.
lines.say: On September sixteenth, the Fed raised rates. And on October first, the US ten-year touched five point three four percent.

lines.text: So what pushed it? Reporting by CNBC, Reuters and Fortune points to four forces.
lines.say: So what pushed it? Reporting by CNBC, Reuters and Fortune points to four main forces.

lines.text: First, oil. With the Strait of Hormuz largely shut, energy prices have kept inflation high.
lines.say: First, oil. With the Strait of Hormuz largely shut, energy prices have kept inflation high.

lines.text: Brent crude topped $108 on Sept 28, after the US rejected an Iranian plan to reopen the strait. It settled at $102.59 on Sept 29.
lines.say: Brent crude topped one hundred eight dollars a barrel on September twenty-eighth, after the US rejected an Iranian plan to reopen the strait. It settled at one hundred two dollars and fifty-nine cents the next day.

lines.text: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge, PCE, was up 3.4% over the year to August, the BEA said on Sept 30.
lines.say: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge, the P C E price index, was up three point four percent over the year to August, the Commerce Department said on September thirtieth.

lines.text: That's well above the Fed's 2% goal. Even without food and energy, it was 3.0%.
lines.say: That's well above the Fed's two percent goal. Even without food and energy, it was three point oh percent.

lines.text: Second, more Fed hikes. Bond traders started betting the Sept 16 hike won't be the last.
lines.say: Second, more Fed hikes. Bond traders started betting the September sixteenth hike won't be the last one.

lines.text: The Fed's own median projection in September put its key rate at 4.1% by the end of 2026, which implies one more hike.
lines.say: The Fed's own median projection in September put its key rate at four point one percent by the end of twenty twenty-six, which implies one more hike.

lines.text: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said: "The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long."
lines.say: At his press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, quote, the plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long.

scene.text: The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long.

lines.text: Third, heavy borrowing. Governments are selling lots of bonds, and buyers want a higher yield to soak them up.
lines.say: Third, heavy borrowing. Governments are selling a lot of bonds, and buyers want a higher yield to soak them all up.

lines.text: Fourth, strong growth, including an AI-fueled investment boom, which keeps demand for money high.
lines.say: Fourth, strong growth, including an A I fueled investment boom, which keeps the demand for borrowed money high.

lines.text: The long end felt it first. On Sept 24, the 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.48%, its highest since 2004, Bloomberg reported.
lines.say: The long end felt it first. On September twenty-fourth, the thirty-year Treasury yield hit five point four eight percent, its highest since two thousand four, Bloomberg reported.

lines.text: It's global. On Oct 1, Germany's 10-year topped 3.6%, the highest since 2008 (Reuters). Britain's topped 5.4%; Japan's hit 3.1%.
lines.say: And it's global. On October first, Germany's ten-year yield topped three point six percent, the highest since two thousand eight, Reuters reported. Britain's topped five point four percent, and Japan's hit about three point one percent.

lines.text: Now, some history. The last time the US 10-year was this high was 2002.
lines.say: Now, a little history. The last time the US ten-year was this high was twenty oh two.

lines.text: Oct 1 also beat the 2007 high, set just before the financial crisis.
lines.say: October first also beat the twenty oh seven high, set just before the financial crisis.

lines.text: In Oct 2023, it briefly topped 5% and then fell back. In 2026, it pushed past that.
lines.say: In October twenty twenty-three, it briefly topped five percent and then fell back. In twenty twenty-six, it pushed right past that.

lines.text: Mortgages aren't at the 2023 peak yet: Freddie Mac's average hit 7.79% on Oct 26, 2023.
lines.say: Mortgages aren't back at their twenty twenty-three peak, though. Freddie Mac's average hit seven point seven nine percent on October twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Winners and losers.
lines.say: So who wins, and who loses?

lines.text: Rising yields split people into two groups: those who borrow, and those who lend or save.
lines.say: Rising yields split people into two groups. Those who borrow, and those who lend or save.

lines.text: Start with home buyers. Here's a hypothetical $400,000, 30-year fixed loan, principal and interest only.
lines.say: Start with home buyers. Here's a hypothetical four hundred thousand dollar, thirty-year fixed loan, counting principal and interest only.

lines.text: At February's 5.98%, the monthly payment is about $2,393.
lines.say: At February's five point nine eight percent, the monthly payment is about two thousand three hundred ninety-three dollars.

lines.text: At Oct 1's 7.28%, the same loan costs about $2,737 a month.
lines.say: At October first's seven point two eight percent, the same loan costs about two thousand seven hundred thirty-seven dollars a month.

lines.text: That's about $344 more every month, or roughly $4,125 a year.
lines.say: That's about three hundred forty-four dollars more every month, or roughly four thousand one hundred twenty-five dollars a year.

lines.text: Over 30 years, total interest goes from about $462,000 to about $585,000.
lines.say: Over thirty years, total interest goes from about four hundred sixty-two thousand dollars to about five hundred eighty-five thousand.

lines.text: The lower rate wins by a mile over the life of the loan.
lines.say: Over the life of the loan, the lower rate wins by a mile.

lines.text: That's about $124,000 more, on the same house, for the same loan.
lines.say: That's about one hundred twenty-four thousand dollars more, for the same house and the same loan.

lines.text: People who already own with an old fixed rate don't pay a cent more. Fixed means fixed.
lines.say: People who already own a home with an old fixed rate don't pay a cent more. Fixed means fixed.

lines.text: The catch: moving means swapping a cheap old rate for a pricier new one, so many owners stay put.
lines.say: The catch is that moving means swapping a cheap old rate for a pricier new one, which is why many owners stay put.

lines.text: That leaves first-time buyers carrying the full weight of 7.28%, with no old cheap loan to fall back on.
lines.say: That leaves first-time buyers carrying the full weight of seven point two eight percent, with no old cheap loan to fall back on.

lines.text: Credit cards and home equity lines usually have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which typically moves with the Fed's rate.
lines.say: Credit cards and home equity lines usually have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which typically moves with the Fed's rate.

lines.text: Now the other side. Savers earn more: on Sept 28, a 4-week Treasury bill yielded 3.96% and a 52-week bill 4.54%.
lines.say: Now the other side. Savers earn more. On September twenty-eighth, a four-week Treasury bill yielded three point nine six percent, and a fifty-two week bill yielded four point five four percent.

lines.text: Locking money up for a year paid more than a month did.
lines.say: Locking money up for a year paid more than a single month did.

lines.text: After the Sept 16 hike, NerdWallet reported savings and CD yields edging up as banks compete for deposits.
lines.say: After the September sixteenth hike, NerdWallet reported savings and C D yields edging up as banks compete for deposits.

lines.text: Example: $10,000 in a 52-week bill at 4.54% earns about $454 over the year, before taxes.
lines.say: Here's an example. Ten thousand dollars in a fifty-two week bill at four point five four percent earns about four hundred fifty-four dollars over the year, before taxes.

lines.text: People buying new bonds also lock in higher yields than they could get in February.
lines.say: People buying new bonds also lock in higher yields than they could get back in February.

lines.text: But people already holding bonds or bond funds saw prices fall as yields rose, the same math as our $900 example.
lines.say: But people already holding bonds or bond funds saw prices fall as yields rose. It's the same math as our nine hundred dollar example.

lines.text: And the government's bill grows: more debt plus higher rates means more of the budget goes to interest.
lines.say: And the government's bill keeps growing. More debt plus higher rates means more of the budget goes to interest.

lines.text: None of this says what rates do next. It's the math of where they were on Oct 1, 2026.
lines.say: None of this says what rates will do next. It's simply the math of where they were on October first.

lines.text: Chapter 5: What to watch.
lines.say: So what's on the calendar?

lines.text: Oct 8: Freddie Mac's next weekly mortgage survey. It comes out every Thursday.
lines.say: October eighth brings Freddie Mac's next weekly mortgage survey. It comes out every Thursday.

lines.text: Oct 14: the BLS releases September's consumer price index at 8:30 a.m. Eastern.
lines.say: On October fourteenth, the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases September's consumer price index at eight thirty in the morning, Eastern.

lines.text: Oct 28: the Fed announces its next rate decision at 2 p.m. Eastern, after a two-day meeting.
lines.say: On October twenty-eighth, the Fed announces its next rate decision at two in the afternoon, Eastern, after a two-day meeting.

lines.text: That October meeting won't include new Fed projections; the next set comes in December.
lines.say: That October meeting won't include a new set of Fed projections. Those come with the December meeting.

lines.text: Dec 11: the current stopgap that funds the federal government runs out.
lines.say: And on December eleventh, the current stopgap bill that funds the federal government runs out.

lines.text: Around all of that: oil and the Strait of Hormuz, which have moved yields all year.
lines.say: Around all of that, there's oil and the Strait of Hormuz, which have moved yields all year long.

lines.text: The number to keep an eye on is the 10-year yield, because mortgages follow it.
lines.say: The number to keep an eye on is the ten-year yield, because mortgages tend to follow it.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap.
lines.say: Let's recap.

lines.text: On Oct 1, 2026, the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34%, the highest since 2002.
lines.say: On October first, the ten-year Treasury yield touched five point three four percent, the highest since twenty oh two.

lines.text: The average 30-year mortgage hit 7.28%, up from 5.98% in late February.
lines.say: The average thirty-year mortgage hit seven point two eight percent, up from five point nine eight percent in late February.

lines.text: Savers and new bond buyers earn more than they did early in 2026.
lines.say: Savers and new bond buyers earn more than they did early in the year.

lines.text: Borrowers, bondholders and the federal budget pay more.
lines.say: Borrowers, existing bondholders and the federal budget all pay more.

lines.text: Same rate, two sides: one person's higher payment is another person's higher interest.
lines.say: It's one rate with two sides. One person's higher payment is another person's higher interest.

lines.text: Subscribe for the week's biggest money story, explained on a whiteboard.
lines.say: If this helped, subscribe for the week's biggest money story, explained on a whiteboard.

post.title: Mortgage rates hit 7.28% on Oct 1. The bond yield behind it, explained
post.ig: On Oct 1, 2026, mortgage rates hit 7.28%. Here's the bond yield behind it.
post.tiktok: Mortgage rates hit 7.28% on Oct 1, 2026. Here's why.
post.yt_desc:
On Oct 1, 2026, Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed mortgage rate hit 7.28%, up from 5.98% on Feb 26, while the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34%, its highest since 2002. This video explains what a bond yield is, why yields climbed (oil and the Strait of Hormuz, the Fed's Sept 16 rate hike, heavy government borrowing and strong growth), and how the US move fits a global bond selloff. It works through a hypothetical $400,000 mortgage, shows who pays more and who earns more, and lists the scheduled dates to watch next.

Sources: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (Feb 26-Oct 1, 2026; Oct 26, 2023); Reuters (Oct 1, 2026); Tradeweb via The Wall Street Journal (Oct 1, 2026); CNBC (Sept 2026); Federal Reserve FOMC statement (Sept 16, 2026); BEA Personal Income and Outlays (Sept 30, 2026); The Conference Board (Sept 29, 2026); CBO Monthly Budget Review (Sept 9, 2026); US Treasury bill rates (Sept 28, 2026); Rio Times and Al Jazeera (Sept 28-29, 2026); Bloomberg (Sept 2026); NerdWallet (Sept 2026); BLS and Federal Reserve calendars.

News and education, not financial advice.
